title: What you still ask

segments.voice: Yesterday, what changed in practice, and your line: it stuck. One habit from this year that stayed. Did you keep it again today, without thinking about it? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

A hand goes up at the back of a study circle, just as everyone is reaching for their shoes. One more question. The teacher sits back down. A year of learning leaves a few of those behind: the verse that still puzzles, the ruling that never quite made sense, the question of why that nobody ever answered. After a year of pillars and schools and chains of narrators, some questions got answered. Others only got sharper. Today is for the sharp ones. Not to close them. To keep them. Questions are welcome here, and the texts themselves say why.
screen: `ONE MORE QUESTION.` → `SOME ANSWERED, SOME SHARPER.` → `QUESTIONS ARE WELCOME.`

segments.voice: First, the book is full of questions. More than once the Qur'an opens a passage with the words they ask thee, yas'alunaka, and then gives an answer. They ask about the new moons. They ask about wine and gambling, and what they should spend. They ask about orphans. They ask about the spirit. People brought real questions, and the questions became part of the book. Second, even a prophet asked. In the Qur'an, Ibrahim says, in paraphrase: my Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He is asked: do you not believe? Yes, he answers, but so that my heart may be at rest. A question is not always doubt. Sometimes it is a heart wanting to settle. Third, not asking can do harm. In a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud, a man with a head wound is told by his companions that they know of no allowance for him to skip washing. He washes, and he dies. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, hears of it, he is angry with them and says, in paraphrase: why didn't they ask, when they didn't know? The cure for not knowing is asking. The Qur'an says it too, in Pickthall's translation: "Ask the followers of the Remembrance if ye know not." Fourth, asking has manners. The same book also says, in paraphrase, don't ask about things that would only trouble you if they were made plain. So the texts do not treat every question the same way. Ask what you need, ask someone who knows, and ask in order to act. In these texts, a question carried well is how learning keeps going.
screen: `THEY ASK THEE: QUESTIONS IN THE BOOK.` · `IBRAHIM ASKS, SO HIS HEART CAN REST.` · `THE CURE FOR NOT KNOWING IS ASKING.` · `ASKING HAS MANNERS TOO.`

segments.voice: The practice: write one for next year. Settle into the sit, and breathe. Let one question rise from this year, the one still standing after the others have gone quiet. It might be about a verse, a ruling, a practice, or something bigger. Don't answer it. Just find the words for it. After the bell, write it down where you'll find it again next year: the back of a notebook, a note on your phone. If you pray, you can set it before Allah in your own words, as a question still open. The bell holds the time.
What you still ask. The question this year left open, kept on purpose, because the texts make room for a question asked in order to learn. Today's word.

Your line: keep asking. Today, ask one person who knows more than you one real question, and listen to the whole answer before you reply. Tomorrow, gratitude for the scholars. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims bring their questions to an imam, a teacher or a scholar, in study circles at the mosque or one to one, and teachers often answer with the verse or hadith behind the answer.

fork.setup: a friend is hurt and asks what the rule is for washing. you aren't sure. what do you do?
options: give the strictest answer you can think of.
say you don't know, and ask someone who does.
fork.reveal: in the hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud, a wounded man was given a confident wrong answer and died. the Prophet said: why didn't they ask, when they didn't know?

original.note: Arabic: they ask thee; the words that open several of the Qur'an's answers.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good believer has no questions left.
what it means: the texts welcome questions asked to learn and to act, and warn against not asking.
what a scholar hears: yas'alunaka passages (2:189, 2:219, 2:220, 17:85), Ibrahim's request in 2:260, and the hadith in Abu Dawud: the cure for not knowing is asking.
recall: a circle that sits to learn
